The Virginia Supreme Court struck down a voter-approved constitutional amendment on procedural grounds, ruling the Legislature had not followed correct procedures when it put the amendment on the ballot.

The Virginia Supreme Court majority held that because over 1.3 million votes had already been cast before the Legislature voted on the proposed amendment on Oct. 31, 2025, the proper constitutional process was not followed.
Republican challengers argued the case involved state courts applying state law and was not one in which the U.S. Supreme Court should intervene, and that federal issues were raised too late.

extractions.title: Justice Clarence Thomas reflects on shared values and his "deeper" friendships on a past court
key_claims: Thomas argued that the ideals in the Declaration of Independence provide common ground for all Americans regardless of religion or location, even under segregation.
Thomas said legal theories like textualism and originalism have 'disenfranchised most people' because most people don't understand them.
Thomas became the second-longest serving justice and could become the longest-serving justice in two years.

Thomas expressed that friendships on the earlier Supreme Court were 'much, much deeper' than those on the current court, crediting the 'greatest generation' justices who valued the institution over themselves.
Thomas noted he had known the four most recent justices — Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, Barrett, and Jackson — when they were law clerks while he was already a sitting justice.

extractions.title: Court rules freight brokers can face negligent hiring suits under state law
key_claims: A unanimous Supreme Court ruled in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state lawsuits claiming they negligently hired dangerous motor carriers.
The case stemmed from a 2017 accident on Illinois Interstate 70 where Shawn Montgomery suffered severe injuries including leg amputation after a tractor-trailer rear-ended his stopped vehicle.

C.H. Robinson, the freight broker, had hired Caribe Transport II despite federal regulators giving the carrier a 'conditional' safety rating for deficiencies in driver qualification, hours of service, and crash rates.

Justice Amy Coney Barrett, writing for the 9-0 court, held that the FAAAA's safety exception in Section 14501(c)(2)(A) applies to negligent hiring claims because they concern motor vehicle safety, preventing preemption.
Barrett clarified that state regulations governing carrier pricing or highway routes would still remain preempted under the FAAAA, limiting the scope of the safety exception.

extractions.title: When (if ever) it's appropriate to make jokes, take selfies, or curse before the court
key_claims: Attorney Geoffrey Pipoly repeated Trump's 'shithole country' comment during oral argument in Mullin v. Doe, a case involving Haitian nationals challenging the revocation of their deportation protections
Justice Sonia Sotomayor chose to say 's-hole country' rather than the full word when referencing the same Trump quote earlier in the argument
The Supreme Court's Guide for Counsel outlines specific protocols including that only the Chief Justice is addressed as 'Mr.' while others are called 'Justice [Last Name]' or 'Your Honor'
Attorneys are required to cease talking immediately when a justice interrupts them, even mid-sentence, and must never interrupt a justice who is speaking
The Guide for Counsel advises attorneys uncertain of a justice's name to use 'Your Honor' rather than risk addressing them by the wrong name

extractions.title: Abortion pill to remain available by mail
key_claims: The Supreme Court granted requests from Danco Laboratories and GenBioPro to pause a 5th Circuit ruling that had reinstated a requirement that mifepristone be dispensed only in person.
Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito wrote dissenting opinions on the abortion pill ruling.
The court unanimously held in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II that negligent hiring claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act.
The Department of Justice accused Yale School of Medicine of violating anti-discrimination laws by favoring Black and Hispanic applicants over white and Asian students.
Watchdog groups urged the Senate to investigate Justice Samuel Alito over oil stock conflicts, following his recusal from a Louisiana case due to financial interest in ConocoPhillips.

extractions.title: Republican legislators urge justices to leave Virginia Supreme Court's redistricting ruling in place
key_claims: The Virginia Supreme Court struck down a constitutional amendment allowing the General Assembly to enact a new congressional map, ruling the referendum invalid because proper procedures were not followed.

The Virginia Supreme Court found that the General Assembly passed the proposed constitutional amendment for the first time after more than 1.3 million votes had already been cast during the 2025 general election.
Voters had approved the constitutional amendment in April by a margin of around three percentage points before it was invalidated.

Republican legislators argue the Supreme Court should not intervene because Virginia Democrats never raised federal law claims before the state courts, only doing so when reaching the U.S. Supreme Court.
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger has indicated Virginia will not use the new 2026 congressional map in upcoming elections, making the point of no return for election preparations moot.

extractions.title: Supreme Court allows for access to abortion pill by mail for now
key_claims: The Supreme Court issued an order blocking a 5th Circuit ruling that had barred the mailing of mifepristone, allowing it to continue to be sent through the mail while litigation continues.
Justice Clarence Thomas dissented, arguing drug companies cannot be irreparably harmed by an order making it harder to 'commit crimes.'
Justice Samuel Alito dissented, calling the order 'remarkable' and arguing it undermines the Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization decision.
In 2024, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled that doctors and medical groups challenging FDA's mifepristone policies lacked standing to sue.
Louisiana sued to reinstate the in-person dispensing requirement, and the 5th Circuit ruled Louisiana has standing and that the in-person requirement should be restored while litigation continues.

extractions.title: The fact of the matter
key_claims: The Supreme Court heard argument in a case involving a jury verdict finding that glyphosate, a key ingredient in Roundup, causes cancer, with Monsanto arguing the jury was not entitled to make such a finding given a federal agency's contrary determination.

Legislative facts (general facts about the world) are distinct from adjudicative facts (the specific who, what, where, and when of individual cases), and both types can arise in individual litigation.
There are no clear rules about when each available method for settling questions of legislative fact is appropriate, creating ambiguity in the judicial system.

Legislative facts can be decided by Congress based on rational speculation, by federal agencies through findings supported by substantial evidence, by the Supreme Court through amicus briefs and independent research, or by juries based on courtroom evidence.
Legislative facts play a significant role in Second Amendment litigation, including questions about the historical meaning of 'arms' in 1791.
